Off the coast of Monterey Bay, California, a giant Pacific octopus navigates a submerged kelp forest. Each arm possesses hundreds of independent suckers capable of tasting chemical cues in the current.

Discover the hidden architecture of kelp forest ecosystems with National Geographic Marine Fellows.
posts.author: National Geographic

posts.text:
High on the rocky cliffs of Svalbard, an arctic fox kit emerges from its subterranean den. In summer months, its coat shifts to mottled grey and brown, providing camouflage among lichen-encrusted boulders.

Witness life on the polar frontier with National Geographic photographers in the High Arctic.
posts.author: National Geographic

posts.text:
Across the vast salt pans of Makgadikgadi in Botswana, thousands of greater flamingos congregate during ephemeral wet seasons. The mineral-rich brine triggers blooms of blue-green algae, transforming the desolate basin into a feeding sanctuary.

Explore our interactive satellite mapping of Southern Africa’s inland wetlands.
posts.author: National Geographic

posts.text:
Deep within the dense canopy of Costa Rica’s rainforest, a red-eyed treefrog rests motionless against a broad palm leaf. By tucking its vibrant orange webbed feet beneath its pale green belly, it renders itself nearly invisible to predatory canopy birds.

National Geographic Explorers are documenting amphibian biodiversity across Mesoamerican wildlife corridors.
posts.author: National Geographic

posts.text:
In a display of sheer determination, this sea otter battles the Pacific surf to haul a heavy boulder from the ocean floor. By balancing the rock on its chest and striking the clam with precision, the otter demonstrates rare tool-use capabilities.

#IncredibleAnimalJourneys is now streaming on Disney+.
posts.author: National Geographic

posts.text:
Much of the land in Cape Froward, Chile, is untamed—and it's set to remain that way when it becomes the 19th national park in Patagonia’s 1,700-mile Route of Parks by the end of 2027. Situated at the southernmost tip of mainland South America, the region offers visitors a chance to learn about the region’s whaling history and the native Kawésqar people as they explore untouched wildness and follow in Charles Darwin's footsteps.

Where do you want to go in 2027? Nat Geo’s #BestOfTheWorld 2027 picks are here and feature iconic destinations for your next adventure. See the full list: https://on.natgeo.com/ie5Fqy

We’re celebrating 20 years of the National Geographic #PhotoArk, an audacious project documenting the world's incredible biodiversity and highlighting the importance of conservation through photography. Which animal do you want to see next?

posts.text:
Puerto Rico's blend of cultures and community-led traditions is sparking renewed interest in the Caribbean Island, and there's no shortage of opportunities to experience it. Beyond its sandy beaches and delicious street food stalls, Loíza is brimming with a rich music history as a bastion for Black Puerto Rican culture, while the Taíno Route and Old San Juan let visitors discover the island's Indigenous and more recent history.

By the 1990s, Siamese crocodiles had disappeared from the wild in Vietnam. Now, conservation efforts are helping the species recover, with an estimated 1,000 mature Siamese crocodiles living across Southeast Asia.

Presented by ROLEX. In Uganda, protecting mountain gorillas starts with keeping their human neighbors healthy. Although their population across East and Central Africa has nearly doubled since the 1990s, diseases passed on by humans remain a serious threat. National Geographic Explorer Gladys Kalema-Zikusoka is working with local communities to reduce that risk and help secure the primates' future.

Through its partnership with the National Geographic Society and as part of its Perpetual Planet Initiative, #Rolex supports expeditions exploring and protecting remarkable places around the world.
